One thing I have been using LFM 2.6 for is annotating emails, text messages, and other metadata. I keep it all ingesting into one giant database and annotate it all as it comes in on an RTX A4500. The LFM annotations are basically triage, and then slowly annotations trickle into my halo model based on lowest confidence (right now that's DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017) for an upgraded annotation. (Agents can then search this database for context).

Excited to roll out LFM 3 to replace it, looks like a big step up. Right now LFM 2.6 gets trustworthy annotations on just over 40% of data points. Just waiting for these to get into LocalAI.

You're doing something similar to what I've been prototyping for the automatic metadata enrichment part. So far I've been using deterministic older techniques + manual for my personal data stream, but I'm trying to learn what the state of the art is for efficiently annotating data with LLMs and newer ML.

This seems interesting, but if anyone else is also doing a similar thing, I'd appreciate tips on how to approach it. So far, I think I have some small RAG model in a demo or the very small qwen models. I think fine tuning seems interesting too. Some of the decision models applied in layers (like a binary search on a pre-generated corpus) could be fast enough to help too?

idk too many options, i'm sure this is a solved problem lol

It's definitely not a solved problem, and it has been kicking my ass. I don't just want metadata tagging/categorization, I want something that identifies the networks between the information, graduates topics to actual objects, and routinely consolidates/synthesizes narratives that can be easily looked up.

SFT -> RL. In our fine-tuning notebooks, we typically say that rollouts that go past the max context length (too much reasoning) get 0 reward, so there is slight pressure for shorter reasoning, but I don't think we have strong regularization. I think the agreed-upon recipe is to first make the model smarter (longer reasoning), then teach it to reason faster/denser.

(I work at Liquid.) Probably, yes. Per the blog, the last 3.5T tokens of pre-training were a mid-training stage with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, and SFT covered tool calling and agentic traces too, because the text model is post-trained to live inside agent harnesses. With an empty system prompt it seems to assume it's in one. I'd try a short system prompt that says no tools are available, and if it still does it, a note on the Hugging Face model page would help the team.

Did y'all do any particular work that makes these models great for moderation? One of the issues between cloud models vs local is that often people are trying to push the limit of what their hardware can do and it doesn't leave too much headroom for moderation to make the models a little more constrained for kids or schools to use locally, or just for family in general who don't want accidental unhinged results.

In the past I've noticed that some LFM were way better at moderation than much larger models. Not necessarily prejudging what is acceptable, but allowing you to interrogate content with a series of questions to customize the moderation. Other models I tested were far worse.

Decision models are like the next optimization in that direction, but none of the benchmarks for the popular models ever show how good they are at tasks like content moderation. The smaller and more efficient we can get that workload, the more that it can simply be on by default in a lot of use cases without feeling like you're giving up a lot of performance, creative freedom or accuracy. You can't have a high number of false positives or people would rather take control back.

We need local content moderation to be cool, efficient, accurate and configurable so that people can get the higher quality results which unsafe models tend to produce, while filtering out the unsafe results fast enough that it can even be done in an agentic way and fed back into the model to steer its results.

on moderation, we run an open guardrail benchmark at raxIT Labs and the hosted d1 models do well. d1.1 is #1 of 30 at checking model output for harmful content (94.4 balanced accuracy), d1-ultra is #1 on harmful user requests (88.2). we haven't run the new 2B open weights yet so no number for those. results and method: https://dm-as-guardrails.raxitlabs.com

This tracks with my experience with their models.  Nice work.  It would be interesting to see what they could do if they optimized even more for moderation like this without going so far as to hurt the model performance overall.

Can you describe more in terms of what moderation you want? I can say with confidence that we don't train for the typical adult-only content you can see on some "de-safe'd" models, but it's not clear to me exactly what you're asking about. We can also discuss over email if you prefer.

I'm largely referring to the fundamental components that can be combined to arrive at a decision. Is this a real life image or text, or is it some sort of art or fiction? Is this in a context of historical events for education, etc? Is this sarcasm? Is this a real threat? Is this nudity? Does this contain violence and gore? Is this suggestive? How old is this character? Is this content sufficiently related to the content it's replying to, or is it spam? Does this response deviate too much from the input request? Is this a business logo?

There was this book called The Inquisitive Mood and it very much reminds me of the chain interrogation process you can do with models now.

This isn't exactly a single use case, it's more like there are use cases for image editing software that use generative models, there are use cases for local LLMs to get a sense for abstract user intent, or to check if a model's action is in line with policy and so on.

As I said, the Liquid AI models are already very good at a lot of this, but considering how good the models are at it, I'm curious how much y'all train on tasks that are moderation-adjacent. If y'all don't have any model that's really specifically trained for these kinds of tasks, it would be interesting to see how close y'all could get if you tried.

This is an actually important problem in the AI space especially for local development.

There are other moderation tasks that are harder, like "is this copyrighted?" or "is this a McDonald's logo?" because of how much copyrighted material there is and how many businesses there are, but it might be possible to get a good feel for "is this likely a trademark?", "is this a business logo?", "does this text seem to describe a popular character?"

To some extent you can combine a model like this with a good database to optimize the filters and identification. Then you can provide a few reference image or text examples that are closer to what you're trying to filter out and the model can say, "yeah, this content is pretty close to your examples."

Google and OpenAI have already released some of their open source safety models and they were really quite bad, from my testing. Yet, Liquid AI hasn't really leaned into promoting their models for moderation purposes despite being excellent. I know there is a lot of political intersection in moderation, especially in the past many years, but I think a model that is smart enough and excels at letting people apply their own rules with fairly good accuracy is important right now.

It all depends on your hardware and throughput requirements. Suppose

1. I were building for my work laptop (M4 Max, 36GB RAM)

2. I had a batched use cases (transcribing + making action items for all meetings in a day)

I would use the LFM3-Audio-2B for ASR (audio -> text transcript) and then LFM3-1.7B for extracting particular action items and adding them to my tool of choice (Linear, Jira, Notes app, etc).

If you can fine-tune (100+ labeled samples, and a GPU), you likely can fine-tune LFM3-Audio-2B for audio -> action items in a single step.

It can also be fine-tuned for specific use cases with SFT/DPO/GRPO. The blog post talks about fine-tuning for wind-turbine classification. No weekends. We need you to get back to work on the next 8B.

It's a model designed to be tiny and still functional, unlike other larger models that are just scaled down and then run into problems (doom loops, intelligence/reasoning failure, tool call failure). You use it when you want a fine-tuned tiny model processing text/audio/video on multiple platforms. (I don't work for them but this is my takeaway)

Disclosure: I work at Liquid. For local agents, LFM3-1.7B fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit, holds 256K context, and was post-trained for harnesses like Hermes Agent and OpenClaw. On WebArena-Verified it goes from 3.0 with LFM2.5-2.6B to 38.4. You can fine-tune it for your own task on one GPU.

Is LFM3-Omni-2B worse or roughly equal at vision tasks compared to LFM3-VL-2B?

In other words: Should I select the model that matches my desired capability set or just use Omni?

unfortunately the models are still stronger without extra modalities. So LFM3-1.7B is better at pure text tasks than all other models. the LFM3-VL-2B is better at text/vision tasks than the Omni, the Audio model is a stronger ASR/TTS model than the Omni, etc.

It's a goal of ours to continue unifying training across modalities so that there is truly one model, instead of just this shared pre-trained backbone.
